title: The Session I Almost Cancelled
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I nearly cancelled my first therapy appointment three times, convincing myself that admitting exhaustion would confirm I had failed at everything I valued.
Narrator: For months I had explained my fatigue away as ambition, as though collapsing into bed each night proved how seriously I took my career.
Narrator: [carefully] It was my sister who finally pointed out that I hadn't laughed properly in longer than either of us could remember.
Narrator: Sitting across from the therapist, I struggled to explain what was wrong, since nothing catastrophic had technically happened to me.
Narrator: [reflective] She asked a question that unsettled me: when was the last time I did something purely because it brought me joy, not results?
Narrator: I could not answer immediately, and the silence that followed embarrassed me more than any admission of sadness would have.
Narrator: [honestly] Over the following weeks, she helped me notice how thoroughly I had tied my worth to output, as if rest had to be earned.
Narrator: I hadn't realized how much resentment had built up beneath my dedication, resentment toward a version of success I had never chosen for myself.
Narrator: [gently] Gradually, I began scheduling things that produced nothing measurable: a walk with no destination, an afternoon reading fiction instead of reports.
Narrator: The guilt during those first unstructured hours was almost physical, a nagging voice insisting I should be doing something more productive instead.
Narrator: [calmly] Slowly, that voice grew quieter, though it never disappeared entirely, and I've learned not to expect it to.
Narrator: My sister noticed the shift before I fully trusted it myself, telling me I sounded lighter on the phone, less braced for disaster.
Narrator: [encouraging] What surprises me most, looking back, is how close I came to dismissing therapy as something reserved for people with more obvious problems than mine.
Narrator: I understand now that burnout rarely announces itself dramatically; it accumulates quietly until ordinary tasks feel unbearably heavy.
Narrator: [seriously] These days, when I notice that familiar tightness returning, I no longer wait for a crisis to justify asking for help again.
Narrator: Healing, I've discovered, is less about fixing something broken and more about learning to notice myself before I break at all.
